contributions.headingText: Tubular carcinoma (TC) is a low-grade invasive carcinoma composed of well-formed tubules with open lumina lined by a single layer of neoplastic cells.
2C60 & XH4TA4 Carcinoma of breast, specialized type & Tubular adenocarcinoma

There are no specific clinical features distinguishing TCs from other types of breast cancer. Nonetheless, TCs are more likely to occur in older patients and tend to be small in size {15247123; 19917872}. Most TCs are detected incidentally by mammographic screening {19917872}. Mammographically, TCs may form a discrete mass, but they are most often detected as small spiculated lesions; calcifications are variably present {16987629; 17420627; 16896563}. On ultrasonography, TC usually appears as a hypoechoic mass with poorly defined margins and posterior acoustic shadowing {16987629; 17420627; 16896563}. MRI data are limited for TCs, but these tumours have been reported as hyperintense, with or without a dark internal septation-like appearance on T2-weighted images {29322118}. Approximately 10–20% of TCs are reported to be multifocal {9199642; 9930775}.

TC accounts for about 1.6% of invasive breast carcinomas (IBCs) {15247123; 9202540; 10334529}. It is a disease of postmenopausal women (67%) {19917872}, with a median patient age at presentation of 63 years; only about 17% of patients with TC are < 50 years old {15247123; 9202540; 10334529}. In the USA, the incidence is slightly higher among white women than among black women {15247123}.
See section Invasive breast carcinoma: General overview .

Gene expression profiling studies demonstrated that TC belongs to the luminal A molecular class of breast cancer {18720457}, which provides a biological basis for the excellent clinical outcome. TCs are typically positive for hormone receptors, and ERBB2 (HER2) is not amplified {16753605}. They also have a low frequency of genomic alterations. Loss-of-heterozygosity and comparative genomic hybridization techniques have demonstrated that the most frequent alterations detected in TC affect 16q (loss; 78–86%) and 1q (gain; 50–62%), and these usually occur concurrently. Other alterations include 16p gain, as well as loss of 8p, 3p (the FHIT gene locus), and 11q (the ATM gene locus) {19675453; 8968105; 18656243; 11230710}. Although these chromosomal alterations are common among other low-grade breast cancers (i.e. low-grade IBC of no special type [NST] and invasive lobular carcinoma), small yet important differences have been detected at the transcriptome level {20593406}.

TCs are characteristically poorly defined spiculated tumours that are firm to hard in consistency and pale grey in colour. Most TCs are small, with a mean diameter of 12 mm {15247123; 9202540}. Approximately 14% of TCs are > 20 mm {10334529; 19917872}.

The diagnosis of TC requires that > 90% of the tumour be composed of tubules and glands lined by a single layer of neoplastic epithelium. Tumours with 10–90% TC are classified as mixed tumours.

At low power, TC has a stellate outline and invades the adjacent normal breast parenchyma. TC is composed of small, round to ovoid or angular glands and tubules with open lumina set within a fibrous or fibroelastotic desmoplastic stroma. The cuboidal to columnar cells that line the neoplastic tubules in a single layer have relatively uniform nuclei of small or intermediate size. Apical snouts may be seen on the luminal aspect of the tubules, and secretions or calcifications may be present in the lumina. TCs are by definition grade 1 carcinomas; if Nottingham grading suggests otherwise, the diagnosis of TC is precluded. Substantial cytological atypia, multilayering, or high mitotic activity excludes the diagnosis of TC.

The tubules in TC have no surrounding myoepithelium, and this is useful in differentiating them from benign conditions such as sclerosing adenosis and radial scar. In these benign conditions, the tubular structures are surrounded by myoepithelium, which can be readily demonstrated by immunohistochemistry for myoepithelial markers such as p63, SMMHC, and high-molecular-weight cytokeratins.

TC may be accompanied by precursor lesions; in a study of 147 tumours and precursor lesions, 95% of pure TCs had associated columnar cell lesions, in particular flat epithelial atypia. Atypical ductal hyperplasia / ductal carcinoma in situ was present in 89% of patients. Colocalization of columnar cell lesions, atypical ductal hyperplasia / ductal carcinoma in situ, and TC was seen in 85% patients with a similar cytological-nuclear morphology in most cases {17325484}. This suggests that a TC might be the result of a multistep process that starts on the level of a flat epithelial atypia.

TC is diffusely and strongly ER-positive and usually also PR-positive. TC is ERBB2 (HER2)-negative {19917872}, and the diagnosis of TC should be reconsidered if a tumour is HER2-positive {29846104}. The cells composing TC have a luminal phenotype (CK8/18-positive, CK5/14-negative) and a low Ki-67 proliferation index (typically < 10%). They are usually positive for E-cadherin but negative for EGFR (HER1), p53, p63, and P-cadherin. Expression of high-molecular-weight cytokeratins and/or ER negativity (especially in small diagnostic biopsies) should raise the possibility of a basal-phenotype carcinoma with tubule formation, such as adenoid cystic carcinoma or low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma. Gene expression profiling places TC into the luminal A group (ER-positive, HER2-negative, low proliferation) {18720457}.

The cytological diagnosis of TC on FNA is problematic. FNA of TC usually yields small tubules and irregular glands lined by relatively bland and uniform epithelial cells in the absence of myoepithelial cells. Although features of malignancy (nuclear atypia, cellular dissociation, and absence of myoepithelial cells) are usually present, the findings are subtle and a definitive diagnosis of malignancy is rendered in only about 50% of cases, even in the hands of experts {2296836; 8173027; 7992574}. Core needle biopsy is a more reliable method of preoperative diagnosis.

Essential: an IBC with > 90% of the tumour consisting of round to ovoid or angular tubules with open lumina, lined by a single layer of epithelial cells with low-grade nuclei and sparse mitosis (grade 1); ER-positive and HER2-negative.

Most TCs present at a relatively early stage. Approximately 86% are T1 tumours and 85% are N0 at presentation {10334529; 19917872}. TCs are staged similarly to other types of IBCs (see section Invasive breast carcinoma: General overview).

In large institutional series {10334529} and cancer registry–based studies {17330844; 14557212; 8001000}, women with TC had an excellent long-term outcome, with reported 5-year survival rates of 88% (overall survival) {10334529} to 96% (relative survival) {8001000}. This is supported by many retrospective cohort studies {18789411; 6289683; 7469549; 17826073; 29413404; 20853056; 19917872; 19386432}. It has been shown that the prognosis of TC is better than that of grade 1 invasive ductal carcinoma {19917872} and that patients’ long-term outcome is similar to that of age-matched women without breast cancer {10334529; 17330844}. Recurrence after complete excision is rare. In some cohorts, axillary involvement was not associated with worse prognosis {10334529}. Given the consistently observed excellent prognosis, it has been suggested that adjuvant systemic therapy or axillary dissection {19917872; 10334529; 11348409; 11412259; 20853056} may not be justified for the routine management of TC.
